items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

A will or letters of administration naming Patrick Flynn as a son would be direct evidence of parentage — upgrading the proof tier from Probable to Proved — and would likely also name Thomas's widow, identifying Patrick's mother (currently unknown). The ps_001 proof summary explicitly flags Thomas Flynn's probate as a primary remaining gap. FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994' (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); Schuylkill County probate volume 007936749 (1851–1930, 412 images) is also browse-only (personCount 0). The county Register of Wills has held probate records since 1811 (loc_001). Date range 1860–1910 is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan: if he had died before 1860, Patrick (age 15) would likely not have remained in the household through the 1860 census; born ~1818, he would reach age 92 by 1910, the outer edge of plausible survival.

FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708–1985. Search for Thomas Flynn's marriage record — which would name Patrick's mother by maiden name — and for baptism entries for Thomas's children, each of which names Thomas as father and typically names the mother as well. The locality guide (loc_001) notes Roman Catholic parishes served the anthracite coal region under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868, then the Diocese of Scranton; sacramental registers survive at the parish and diocesan level. Date range 1838–1870: marriage before Patrick's ~1845 birth, children's baptisms through the years the family was active in Schuylkill County. Search variant spellings: Flynn, Flinn, Flin.

Fallback if the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH name search (item 2, pli_007) yields no results for Thomas Flynn. The locality guide (loc_001) explicitly warns that some anthracite-region church films are browse-only image groups with ~0% record-searchable. Volume 007936751 (imageGroupNumber 007936751, 1842–1895, 187 images, browse-only, personCount 0) covers church records in both English and German and is not name-searchable; the Flynn household's Catholic parish registers may appear here. Browse image-by-image, focusing on the 1838–1870 window for Thomas Flynn's marriage and children's baptisms.

Patrick's marriage record may list his parents' names — a practice standard in Catholic sacramental registers and common on civil marriage returns. Schuylkill County marriage records volume 007936753 (1870–1910, 94 images, browse-only, personCount 0) covers the civil record series; the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH indexed collection (item 2) will capture any church marriage entry found during that search. Date range 1865–1895: Patrick born ~1845, most likely married between age 20 and 50. Note: the civil volume begins 1870; if Patrick married before 1870, the record will only appear in parish registers (items 2–3). Search variant spellings: Flynn, Flinn, Flin.

The preponderance of evidence (1850 and 1860 census birthplace: Ireland, accepted over the secondary-informant death certificate's 'Pennsylvania') indicates Patrick was born in Ireland and emigrated. A naturalization declaration of intent or petition from Schuylkill County's Court of Common Pleas would state his birth date, birth country, and date and port of arrival — information that could narrow the Irish county of origin and help locate his baptism record there. Schuylkill County naturalization records volume 007936750 (1849–1915, 298 images, browse-only, personCount 0). Date range 1863–1895: Patrick would have filed no earlier than ~1863 (reaching majority at ~18), with most naturalizations completed within 5–7 years of arrival.

Required FAN item for a parentage question. In Irish Catholic immigrant communities in the anthracite coal region, baptism sponsors (godparents) and marriage witnesses were almost always relatives or co-migrants from the same Irish county or townland — making them a route to the family's Irish place of origin and to identifying Thomas Flynn's wife's maiden name. Once Thomas Flynn's marriage and children's baptisms are located via items 2–3, the named witnesses should be searched in SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable, personCount 982,415): their own records may corroborate the Flynns' Irish origins or name Thomas's wife's parents directly. This item depends on items 2 or 3 producing at least one record with named witnesses, and should execute after those items.

### Item-by-item rationale

**Step 1 — pli_006: 1880 Federal Census (FamilySearch)**
The 1880 census is the first U.S. enumeration to state each person's relationship to the head. Thomas (b. ~1818) would be ~62 — plausibly alive. Any child listed as "son" or "daughter" in his household gives **stated-relationship evidence** for paternity, far stronger than the inferred co-residence in 1850 and 1860. The household also names Thomas's wife — the only route to Patrick's mother since she appears nowhere in the project. Search variants: Flynn, Flinn, Flyn.

**Step 2 — pli_007: 1880 Federal Census (Ancestry, fallback)**
Independent index; may catch transcription variants missed by FamilySearch. Execute only if pli_006 yields nothing.

**Step 3 — pli_008: Thomas Flynn's marriage, Schuylkill County Church Records**
A **dedicated parentage-question item** for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. The collection is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). The Flynns were almost certainly Catholic; per the locality guide, parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868, then Scranton. The couple may have married in Ireland (before Patrick was born there ca. 1845), but any Pennsylvania marriage would name the wife. The mother's surname from this entry may be her birth surname, or a prior married name if she remarried — a companion search (pli_009) tests that.

**Step 4 — pli_009: Siblings' baptisms + Patrick's marriage (same Church Records collection)**
*(a)* Catholic baptisms name both parents. The 1860 census shows Patrick as child_2, so at least one sibling was older; younger Pennsylvania-born siblings would be baptized in Schuylkill County parishes. Each baptism is **direct parentage evidence** for that sibling and the first independent naming of the mother.
*(b)* Search Patrick Flynn as a groom ca. 1865–1885: groom's parents are often recorded in Catholic marriage registers, which would directly name Thomas as Patrick's father.

**Step 5 — pli_010: Thomas Flynn's probate (browse-only)**
The Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 is **browse-only (personCount 0)** — requires image-by-image browsing of Schuylkill County docket books. S4 ("Schuylkill County Probate Records") has sat in the tree since day one without ever being searched. Thomas (b. ~1818) had a plausible death window of 1861–1910; date range is set by his lifespan, not Patrick's. A will naming Patrick as son or heir is the **most direct paternity evidence** achievable through FAN sources.

**Step 6 — pli_011: 1870 Federal Census (FamilySearch)**
Bridge census. Thomas (~52 in 1870) almost certainly still alive. While 1870 doesn't state relationships, a consistent family unit across 1860→1870→1880 confirms Thomas as a single identifiable individual and supplies the wife's name for targeted church searches.

**Step 7 — pli_012: Thomas Flynn's naturalization, Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas**
Thomas arrived before 1850 and almost certainly naturalized. Declarations of intent and petitions sometimes list the wife and children by name. At minimum, naturalization papers corroborate Thomas's specific identity and may record his Irish county of origin — enabling an Irish parish search if Pennsylvania evidence proves insufficient.

**Step 8 — pli_013: Siblings' Pennsylvania death certificates (post-1906)**
Pennsylvania state registration began 1906. Siblings born ca. 1835–1860 would be 46–71 at the start of registration — many still living in the coal region. A sibling's death certificate names **both parents**, providing independent corroboration of Thomas as father and the first confirmed maiden name (or prior married name) of Patrick's mother. This item depends on siblings identified in pli_006, pli_009, and pli_011; its date window is set by the siblings' plausible lifespan.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024; name-searchable, personCount 38,558,371). The next unsearched enumeration after pl_002's 1860 search. Thomas Flynn would be approximately 52 in 1870; Patrick approximately 25. Searching both names (and the Flinn spelling variant) in Schuylkill County will show whether they still share a household and — critically — may surface Thomas's wife, whose name no source searched to date has supplied. The 1870 census does not state household relationships (that column was not introduced until 1880), but listing a woman alongside Thomas and Patrick provides a name to pursue in church marriage and probate records. If Patrick has left the household by 1870, his separate entry still confirms his continued presence in the county and may show a new household with relatives.

United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683; name-searchable, personCount 50,169,452). The 1880 census is the highest-value census item in this plan: it is the first U.S. enumeration to include a relationship-to-head column. Thomas Flynn would be approximately 62 in 1880; Patrick approximately 35. If Thomas is found, the relationship of each household member to him is directly stated — a finding that would advance the parentage conclusion from 'probable' toward 'proved' for the father-son link. The wife's relationship to Thomas would also be explicit, for the first time naming Patrick's mother as a recorded fact rather than an inference. Also search for Patrick Flynn as a separate household head; any co-resident kin and the stated relationship column would further corroborate the family network.

United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221; name-searchable, personCount 76,211,837). The 1890 census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire and cannot be searched, making 1900 the next available enumeration after 1880. Thomas Flynn, born ~1818, would be approximately 82 in 1900 — possible but death before this date is equally plausible. Search Thomas first; if absent, search Patrick's own household (approximately 55 in 1900). The 1900 census records both the month and year of birth and years of immigration, which may pinpoint the Irish county of origin — a lead toward Irish baptismal records that could confirm parentage independently. If Thomas is found, the relationship column again directly corroborates the father-son link.

Required item for a parentage plan: a dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; name-searchable, personCount 982,415; covering 1708–1985). Thomas was born ~1818 in Ireland and was already settled in Schuylkill County by 1850; a marriage in the 1835–1848 window is plausible before Patrick's birth ~1845. The locality guide (loc_001) notes Roman Catholic parishes in the county fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868. The marriage record would: (a) confirm Thomas and his wife as a couple; (b) supply the mother's maiden name, which no source searched to date has provided — her identity is entirely unknown; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth ~1845, corroborate Thomas as Patrick's father, whose naming currently rests on a secondary informant (the death certificate's son-in-law). Note: the marriage record alone does not place Patrick with this couple; that link still rests on the census co-residence and the death certificate; the marriage strengthens the case but cannot stand as its sole basis.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196; browse-only, personCount 0). The locality guide (loc_001) confirms Schuylkill County probate records are held by the Register of Wills from 1811 and are a primary parentage source naming heirs. Thomas Flynn was born ~1818; his plausible lifespan sets this window's bounds — 1860 is the lower bound (the year of the last searched census), and 1900 is the outer bound of a reasonable lifespan for someone born in 1818. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence, the strongest single item obtainable short of a baptism record. An intestate administration file naming the heirs is equally useful. Because this is a browse-only image collection (personCount 0), the researcher must page through Schuylkill County probate dockets by year range rather than running a name search.

FAN item — required for a parentage question. The 1860 census extraction recorded Patrick as 'child_2' in Thomas Flynn's household, implying at least one other child was present in that enumeration. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; name-searchable, personCount 982,415). Search for Flynn (and Flinn) baptisms in Schuylkill County Catholic registers between 1838 and 1870 — a range bounded by Thomas's plausible marriage date and the end of his likely child-rearing years. A baptism entry for a sibling of Patrick would name both Thomas Flynn and his wife, including her maiden name as stated at the font — the most direct route to the mother's identity given that neither census lists her explicitly. Evidence about Patrick's parentage derived from a sibling's record is indirect but independent of the census co-residence and the secondary death-certificate informant, and corroborates the overall case.

**Tree survey (I1 — María Josefa García Romero):** No sources, no parents, no spouse, no children. Born ~1843, Vélez-Málaga. Nothing in the tree answers the question.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

John Doyle's probate, when found, may name all surviving children as heirs. The plan sweeps census years 1850–1910, then church and probate browse-only films, then marriage records, then a FAN search on the known child Ellen Doyle, and finally a cemetery search for the family burial plot. Search with surname variants (Doyel, O'Doyle) and a broad age range for Bridget (~25–50). Browse the Schuylkill County probate dockets under 'Doyle' and variants. A will is direct evidence; letters of administration naming a widow as administratrix corroborate his death date and surname.

Volume 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records, 1870–1910) is browse-only (personCount 0, 0% indexed). The date window 1870–1930 spans the most likely range of Ellen's marriage and death. Search FindAGrave for the Doyle family burial plot in Schuylkill County Catholic cemeteries (e.g., St. Patrick's in Pottsville, or the cemetery associated with the Doyles' home parish). Browse the 1779 baptism section; the entry will directly name both parents — the fastest route to the father's full name. 'Blyeberg' is a farm-name locator denoting residence, not a hereditary surname (loc_001 quirk; Denmark Naming Customs wiki); 'Mikkel' may appear as 'Michel' or 'Michael' in the register.

Danish lægdsruller enroll every male from birth under his father's name — direct parentage evidence per loc_001 quirk (Denmark Military Records wiki confirms records of genealogical value begin ~1788). Mikkel (born 1779) would appear under father 'Niels' in the earliest rolls from 1789. Collection 2513529 (Denmark, Military Levying Rolls, 1789-1861) is name-searchable (personCount 200408); however, the Thisted Amt volume 004748896 (1789–1814, 1204 images) is browse-only (personCount 0). Search the indexed collection first; if Mikkel is not found for the Thisted district, browse volume 004748896. Each roll entry records the conscript's name, father's name, birthplace, and age — multiple data points to confirm identity.

A dedicated item for the parents' marriage is required on every parentage plan (record-type-guide). The marriage: (a) confirms the couple as a unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, omitted by census and death records; (c) corroborates the father named in the baptism entry (item 1) by showing the couple's union predates Mikkel's birth. Browse volume 004130616 (Stagstrup, 1763–1814, browse-only at ~3% indexed) for marriage entries from 1763 through 1779, searching for a groom named 'Niels.' Note: the marriage record alone does not prove Mikkel is their child — that link requires item 1.

The 1787 census (collection 1401625, name-searchable personCount 21033401) records household composition with ages and relationships. Mikkel would be approximately 8 years old and living with his parents; searching under his father's given name 'Niels' in Stagstrup may be needed if Mikkel himself is not the indexed head. The 1801 census (same collection) shows Mikkel at ~22, and his father may still head the household if alive. Also accessible via Dansk Demografisk Database (https://ddd.dda.dk/ddd_en.htm), which provides free transcriptions of the 1787 and 1801 Danish censuses.

The second part of the objective is to determine when the father died. A skifteprotokol (estate/probate record) filed at the father's death would name him, his heirs (potentially including Mikkel), and give a death date. Collection 2015318 (Denmark, Probate Indexes, 1674-1851) is name-searchable (personCount 1310442). Search for 'Niels' of Stagstrup or the Blyeberg farm in the Hassing Herred or Thisted district. Date range 1779–1840 is set by the father's plausible lifespan after Mikkel's birth in 1779 — a father of a child born that year could plausibly die anywhere from 1779 to ~1840 — not by Mikkel's own research window.

Fallback browse if collection 2015318 (item 5) returns nothing for the father. Volume 004392710 covers Hassing Herred skifteprotokoller 1690–1850 and is browse-only (personCount 0, 655 images). If the father's death date is already established from items 1 or 7, focus the browse on that decade; otherwise browse broadly for 'Niels' of Stagstrup/Blyeberg across 1779–1840.

The father's burial entry in the Stagstrup kirkebog will directly record his death date and typically gives his age — enabling a birth-year estimate and confirming identity. Browse volume 004130616 (1763–1814) for burial entries naming 'Niels' of Stagstrup/Blyeberg. The volume runs only to 1814; if the father lived past 1814, a subsequent Stagstrup volume must be identified and browsed. This item is sequenced after items 1–4 so the father's full name is known before the burial section is searched.

FAN item required for a parentage question (BCG Standard 14). Other children of the same father 'Niels' baptized in Stagstrup will each name the same parents, corroborating Mikkel's parentage and identifying the full sibling set. The Danish naming pattern (first son named for paternal grandfather, second for maternal grandfather — Denmark Naming Customs wiki) may reveal the paternal grandfather's given name. Godparents in sibling entries are often kin and supply further FAN leads. Browse volume 004130616 (1763–1814) for all baptisms naming 'Niels' as father in Stagstrup, from the register's start in 1763 through ~1800.

Rigsarkivet arkivalieronline provides free access to browse original images of Thisted Amt church books at https://www.sa.dk/ao-soegesider/en/other/other-collection/16. Alternate route if FamilySearch volume 004130616 images are unclear or coverage differs. The researcher must open that URL, select Thisted Amt, navigate to Stagstrup parish, and browse year by year. Useful for verifying reads from items 1, 3, 7, and 8.

Rigsarkivet arkivalieronline provides free browsable images of the lægdsruller for Thisted Amt at https://www.sa.dk/ao-soegesider/en/other/index-creator/71. Alternate route if the FamilySearch collection 2513529 index misses Mikkel in the Thisted district or if volume 004748896 images are difficult to read. The researcher must open that URL and navigate to the Thisted/Stagstrup levy district.
